solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Smooth seed oddly ignored near bird

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered positions leaves only the second and fourth letters of the word

blocks.note: to sand wood is to smooth it
a pip is the seed of an apple or orange
the even letters of this word

explanation.surface: Someone smoothing ground, scattering seed unevenly beside a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' looks like an adjective but works as a verb, as with sandpaper. 'Oddly ignored' keeps only the even letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandpiper is a small wading shorebird found along beaches and mudflats.

clue.text: Laughing uproariously seeing Carry On film?

blocks.note: first meaning: in fits of loud laughter
second meaning: the title word of a 1966 entry in the Carry On series

explanation.walkthrough: The Carry On films are a long-running series of bawdy British comedies; one is called Carry On Screaming!, a horror spoof.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone helpless with laughter is said to be screaming, and the comedy title supplies the same word as a proper name.

clue.text: At no time software vendor is saving for retirement

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it inside, so the letters are held within the words
retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A tech company that never puts money into its staff pension fund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saving for retirement' reads as pension planning, but it splits into a hidden indicator and a reversal indicator: the letters sit across softwaRE VENdor, read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the phrase and the adverb mean on no occasion whatsoever, an exact synonym.

clue.text: Criticise revolutionary adopting American style

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in and give a home, so one piece is taken inside the others

blocks.note: critics pan a show they dislike
A is the abbreviation for American
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: Attacking a radical who has taken on an American way of doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: Che Guevara is the crossword's favourite revolutionary; the American slips in between the criticism and him.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is flamboyant confidence and flair, the same quality as stylishness in manner.

clue.text: Sumptuous large Indian dish, not starter, and drink served up

indicators.note: without its starter means the opening letter is dropped
in a down clue, anything served up is brought upwards, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
raita, the yoghurt side dish, minus its first letter
a cat will lap up milk

explanation.surface: A lavish curry-house order: a big side dish without its starter course, with a drink brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: Raita is a cooling yoghurt-and-cucumber dish served with curries. Everything from 'large' to 'drink' is joined, then the whole string is read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Palatial means like a palace, splendid and luxurious, so it matches lavishly grand surroundings.

clue.text: Lax about way of addressing schoolteacher

blocks.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
pupils call a female teacher Miss

explanation.surface: Someone being casual about how pupils speak to their teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' is the Latin-derived RE, not a container or reversal indicator here.
explanation.definitionFit: Being remiss is being careless or negligent about one's duties, which is slack behaviour.

clue.text: Chunk of wood cut after turning

indicators.note: cutting something short trims off its final letter
turning round makes the letters face the other way

blocks.note: balsa is a very light wood used by model-makers

explanation.surface: A block of timber trimmed after being turned on a lathe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chunk of wood' looks like the definition, but 'wood' is the wordplay: shortened balsa, then flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A slab is a thick flat piece of material, a broad lump or block.

clue.text: What MPs do when member is deceased?

blocks.note: a limb is a member of the body
taken as written
the late Mr Smith is the deceased one

explanation.surface: What Parliament does when one of its members dies, such as holding a by-election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' plays on Member of Parliament, but here it is a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament make laws, which is exactly the job of passing legislation.

clue.text: Times runs number that’s upset poet

indicators.note: upset means tipped over, which in a down clue turns the letters upside down

blocks.note: three by four means three times four
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs
No. is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a poet getting upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is multiplication.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Byron was the Romantic poet who wrote Don Juan, a famous example of the type.

clue.text: Manages entertaining live artist

indicators.note: a host entertaining guests has them inside the house

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: An agent who handles a performing artist's live shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live' suggests a gig but is the verb to exist.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Paul Rubens was a Flemish Baroque painter, an example of the category.

clue.text: Split with pal discovered smuggling valuables primarily

indicators.note: dis-covered means with its covering taken off, so the outer letters go
primarily means in the first place, so only the opening letter is wanted
smuggled goods are hidden inside something, so one piece is carried within another

blocks.note: a pal is a friend
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A falling-out with a friend who was caught smuggling valuables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Split with pal' reads as a break-up, but 'with' is only a link: the definition is 'Split' alone, and the pal loses both ends before taking in the V.
explanation.definitionFit: Riven is the old past participle of rive, meaning torn apart or divided, so it means cleft.

clue.text: Flexible, purchasing for the most part fancy cheese

indicators.note: purchasing means taking hold of and acquiring, so one piece gets held inside another
only most of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped

blocks.note: limber means supple
a fancy for something is a desire or urge

explanation.surface: A supple shopper buying mostly fancy cheeses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like an adjective describing the cheese, but it is a noun meaning desire, shortened and tucked into the word for supple.
explanation.definitionFit: Limburger is a soft, notoriously smelly Belgian cheese, so it is one example of the dairy product.

clue.text: Pound off exotic tropical fruit

indicators.note: off means taken away, so that letter is removed
something exotic is strange and unusual, so the letters take an unfamiliar arrangement

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound sterling, from Latin libra
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop knocking a pound off the price of exotic tropical fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound off' reads as a discount, but it means remove the L. 'Tropical fruit' looks like one phrase, yet 'tropical' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit, an example of the general class.

clue.text: Crushes spouse’s offspring

definitions.note: a verb phrase in the third person, split as two words

blocks.note: first meaning: treads on, squashing underfoot
second meaning: a husband's or wife's boy from an earlier relationship

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a parent dealing with a partner's child; the same letters split two ways give a verb phrase and a family relation.
explanation.definitionFit: Treading on something squashes it, and a husband's or wife's son by another partner is a stepchild.

clue.text: Naked, removing last of alluring loose nightwear

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter
removing means taking out, so that letter is struck from the fodder
loose means not held in place, so the letters are free to move around

blocks.note: the final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shedding seductive, loose-fitting nightclothes and ending up naked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alluring loose nightwear' reads as a negligee, but 'alluring' only supplies its G, which comes out of the nightwear before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the raw is an informal idiom for wearing no clothes at all.

clue.text: Sign he’s invested in something a setter uses

indicators.note: money invested in a firm is put inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
Taurus the bull is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: An astrology column hinting that a certain man has put money into a crossword setter's tools.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'he’s' is ignored, so the letters HES go inside the star sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter hunting for synonyms reaches for a reference book listing words of similar meaning.

clue.text: Handle entry of mine

blocks.note: first meaning: the long stem of a tool such as a spade or golf club
second meaning: the vertical passage leading down into a pit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a verb and 'mine' like a possessive pronoun, as if someone manages their own entry; both are nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool's long gripping pole and the vertical access tunnel into a colliery share this one word.

clue.text: Poor Richard and Georgia, say, put emojis in emails?

definitions.note: an example of the plural class

blocks.note: first meaning: two computer fonts named for people
second meaning, read as a verb phrase: keying in little smiling pictures

explanation.surface: A pair of people, one hard-up, using smileys in their email.
explanation.walkthrough: Poor Richard and Georgia read as two people but are both font names. The question mark flags the playful second reading: you type faces when you add emojis.
explanation.definitionFit: Fonts are designs of lettering, and keying in smiley icons is literally keyboarding little heads.

clue.text: Convict peeping Tom, filled with scorn at intervals

indicators.note: something filled with stuff has it packed inside
taking letters at intervals means every other one

blocks.note: a peeping Tom pries into others' lives
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A voyeur found guilty and despised by everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convict' could be the verb, but it is the noun: a peeping Tom is a nosy person, one who pries.
explanation.definitionFit: A convict is someone serving a sentence in jail, an inmate.

clue.text: Horses eat grass audibly

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the word is identified by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: cattle and horses graze in a field

explanation.surface: Horses munching grass in a field, noisily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horses eat grass' is a plain picture; 'Horses' is the definition and the rest is the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey horses, white or pale-coated animals, are called greys, like the Royal Scots Greys cavalry.

clue.text: Booted partner from clubs, maybe extremely enraged

definitions.note: describes the word that pairs with booted, not a synonym of it

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends

blocks.note: clubs is one of the four card suits
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A furious club member throws out their partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booted' suggests being kicked out, but it points to the phrase suited and booted, meaning smartly dressed; the answer is booted's partner in that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: In the British expression suited and booted, describing someone dressed up, the two words always appear together.

clue.text: Recall party at Westminster socialist George vacuously interrupts

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside is emptied and just the outer letters stay
something that interrupts breaks into the middle of another

blocks.note: the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland, which has MPs at Westminster
red is the colour of socialism
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A socialist MP called George heckling a party conference in Parliament with empty remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: Westminster is the UK Parliament; the DUP is a Northern Irish party sitting there. 'Recall' sounds like a political recall petition, but it means bring back to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To dredge up a memory is to haul it back from the depths, an idiom for remembering.

clue.text: Film about hotel I dread being remade

indicators.note: remaking something means building it again in a new form

blocks.note: H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic afraid that a movie set in a hotel is getting a remake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being remade' fits films, which is the misdirection: it shuffles the letters. 'About' is only a link meaning concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: Die Hard is the 1988 Bruce Willis action movie, an example of the general category.

clue.text: Raised spray-can, it apparently maintains sheen

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters makes them read bottom to top
to maintain is to hold, so the letters are held within the phrase

blocks.note: spanning the end of the first, the middle word and the start of the last

explanation.surface: An aerosol held up, supposedly keeping a shine on something.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across spray-cAN IT APparently, read upwards. 'Apparently' does double duty, contributing its first letters as well as the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is the glossy film that forms on old bronze or polished wood, a surface lustre.

clue.text: Energy of creatures heading west, needing time for meal finally

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west is moving right to left
finally means at the end, so only the closing letter counts
needing one thing in place of another means a swap

blocks.note: animals are creatures
final letter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Migrating animals needing their final meal to keep going.
explanation.walkthrough: The animals reversed give SLAMINA; then the L from meal makes way for T.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is staying power, the physical capacity to keep going, close to vigour.

clue.text: Muscle stitch, pinching pain Dad overlooked

indicators.note: to pinch is to grip between fingers, so one piece is held within another
something overlooked is left out, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: to stitch is to sew
taken as written
pa is a word for father

explanation.surface: A muscle stitch, a sharp pain Dad ignored while running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muscle stitch' reads as one phrase about a runner's cramp; 'stitch' is the wordplay, not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinew is tendon, the tissue joining muscle to bone, and loosely means muscular strength.

clue.text: Western peacekeeper lacking cover marshals international forces

indicators.note: with its cover gone, a word has lost its outer layer, its first and last letters

blocks.note: to marshal people is to usher them
I is the abbreviation for international
F stands for force, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A cowboy lawman without backup gathering an international force.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marshals' tempts as a lawman synonym, but it is a verb meaning ushers; the definition is 'Western peacekeeper'.
explanation.definitionFit: In cowboy films the sheriff is the town lawman who keeps order in the Wild West.

clue.text: Parking behind this writer’s Tesla regularly in drive

indicators.note: behind means coming after, so this piece is placed following the other in the answer
regularly means at even spacing, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: the setter speaking: I am, shortened
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A columnist parking behind their own electric car in the driveway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer’s' is the setter saying I'M, and P goes behind it. 'Drive' looks like the driveway but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel is to push or urge forward, the same as to propel someone into action.

clue.text: European in on wager that’s improper

indicators.note: improper means not correct, so the letters are in the wrong order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A continental involved in a dodgy bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European' could be any nationality; the nine letters of the wager phrase settle which.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Norway is a Scandinavian, and so belongs to the continent's peoples.

clue.text: Bill takes turn briefly making jelly

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside
said briefly means cut short, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
a spin is a turn

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill having a quick go at making a jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name but is an account, abbreviated AC. 'Turn' is a rotation, not a go.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury gelatine made from meat stock, used to set cold dishes.

clue.text: Originally wartime remains bear investigation

definitions.note: a verb phrase meaning stand up to scrutiny

indicators.note: originally means at the origin or start, so the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter
ashes are what remains after burning or cremation

explanation.surface: Wartime human remains being examined by investigators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' reads as a verb or as bodies, but means ash. The definition is idiomatic: an excuse that won't wash fails to convince.
explanation.definitionFit: A story that washes holds up when examined, an idiom for being believable under scrutiny.

clue.text: Ladies are crazy for dogs

indicators.note: crazy means wild and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Women who are mad about their pet dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy for' reads as mad about; 'crazy' is the anagram signal and 'for' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Airedales are large terriers from Yorkshire, an example of canine breeds.
